overview: This two-document file concerns a June 1946 inquiry by the New York law firm Willkie Owen Otis Farr & Gallagher on behalf of Ipekdjian Brothers, diamond importers and exporters seeking the recovery of diamonds left in the Netherlands Indies during the Japanese invasion and believed to have been transported to Japan. The attorneys ask the U.S. Department of State to identify the agency responsible for diamonds found by American occupation forces and to provide access to an inventory. The accompanying State Department form requests information about the citizenship of the interested parties and the extent of non-American ownership in Ipekdjian Brothers before the claim can be investigated. Although catalogued under “Radium,” the surviving material deals with diamonds, wartime seizure, and postwar property restitution.

subfiles.title: Letter requesting assistance in locating Ipekdjian Brothers’ diamonds
subfiles.from: Simon J. Nusbaum, Willkie Owen Otis Farr & Gallagher
subfiles.to: Department of State, Foreign Service Administration
subfiles.about: The attorney for Ipekdjian Brothers asks which U.S. agency controls diamonds found in Japan that may have been seized from the firm in the Netherlands Indies.
subfiles.summary: Ipekdjian Brothers owned a substantial stock of diamonds in the Netherlands Indies before the Japanese invasion but was unable to move them to New York in time. The firm subsequently learned that American occupation forces had found a large stock of diamonds in Japan identified as originating in the Netherlands Indies. Nusbaum asks the State Department to identify the responsible agency, permit submission of identifying particulars, and explain where an inventory of the recovered stock may be consulted.

subfiles.title: State Department request for additional information on Ipekdjian Brothers
subfiles.to: Ipekdjian Brothers case representatives; exact addressee not shown
subfiles.about: The Department requests citizenship and ownership information needed to investigate the Ipekdjian Brothers property claim.
subfiles.summary: A standard State Department property-interest form states that further information is essential before a full reply can be made. The checked items request the citizenship details of the interested parties and the nature and extent of non-American interests in Ipekdjian Brothers. The form also lists other possible evidentiary categories—property descriptions, title, bank deposits, estates, overseas attorneys, and evidence of enemy seizure—and specifies the number of copies required for claims involving Germany or other countries.

interest: The file offers a compact example of how private businesses attempted to recover movable assets looted or displaced within the Japanese wartime empire. It links a specific diamond claim to the broader work of American occupation authorities inventorying valuables found in Japan, while the standardized reply reveals the citizenship and ownership tests used by the State Department in processing postwar claims. The mismatch between the archival heading “Radium” and the documents’ actual focus on diamonds is also useful evidence of the imperfections and broad categorization practices of the decimal filing system.
